jurisdiction: United States — federal layer only (no state law analysed; see "state-law preemption reality" below). Corrected copy: this file supersedes lane-1-UnitedStatesfedera.brief.json after application of lane-1.audit.json.
headline: Federal law never makes any of these four models lawful — UIGEA, the Illegal Gambling Business Act and the Travel Act are all derivative of state law and 31 U.S.C. § 5361(b) expressly disclaims preemption — so the only genuinely independent federal gates are (1) FinCEN money-transmitter registration, which Model B triggers outright and Model C triggers if you hold withdrawable user balances; (2) the federal wagering excise tax under 26 U.S.C. §§ 4401/4411/4412, which is a real filing question for any paid-entry model but which the IRS's own cited authority treats FAVOURABLY for an operator-funded fixed-prize skill contest — AM 2020-009 applied the tax to daily fantasy sports precisely because the DFS entrant does not control the outcome, and it endorses Rev. Rul. 57-521, 1957-2 C.B. 779, holding that an entry fee in a contest of mental skill with a guaranteed operator-funded prize is NOT a wager unless the entry fees alone comprise the prize [CORRECTED: the original brief called excise tax 'the under-appreciated killer' and said no authority existed — both refuted]; and (3) consumer-protection exposure under FTC Act § 5 and COPPA, to which must be added a separate and larger private-litigation gate: Skillz Platform Inc. v. Papaya Gaming, Ltd. (S.D.N.Y., judgment 28 July 2026) was a COMPETITOR suit under the Lanham Act and New York GBL, not an FTC action; it is an un-appealed-as-yet district-court judgment that binds no one, and its $719m disgorgement figure is an ALTERNATIVE remedy the plaintiff may elect in lieu of the $420m April 2026 jury verdict, not an addition to it. Undisclosed bot opponents in a paid duel remain the single most dangerous fact pattern for FACT//DUEL regardless of who can sue.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: Closed-loop cosmetic coins are not a 'bet or wager' under 31 U.S.C. § 5362(1)(A): the user stakes nothing on the outcome of 'a contest of others, a sporting event, or a game subject to chance', and receives nothing of value on any outcome. No prize of value means no lottery (no prize/chance/consideration triad), so 18 U.S.C. §§ 1301-1304 are not engaged. The Wire Act reaches only 'bets or wagers' and (per the First Circuit) only sporting events — not engaged. 18 U.S.C. § 1955 requires an underlying state gambling-law violation and a 'gambling business' — not engaged. CORRECTED (audit defect 7): the § 5362(1)(E)(viii) exclusion does NOT support purchased coins. Clause (viii) covers participation where participants 'do not stake or risk anything of value other than — (I) personal efforts ... or (II) points or credits that the sponsor of the game or contest provides to participants FREE OF CHARGE'. Model A coins are bought for dollars, so (viii) is unavailable the moment coins are sold; it continues to cover only the existing free demo-coin game. Model A's real federal argument is the § 5362(1)(A) 'nothing of value staked, no prize of value' point, standing alone. On money transmission, the coin is NOT a convertible virtual currency: FinCEN FIN-2019-G001 § 1.3 defines CVC as virtual currency that 'either has an equivalent value as currency, or acts as a substitute for currency', and a coin that can never be redeemed for money or a prize of value is neither. Independently, the operator accepts funds only integral to the sale of its own (non-money-transmission) service and so falls in the exemption at 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(ii)(F). If instead characterised as prepaid access, a closed-loop arrangement limited to $2,000 of value per device per day is not a 'prepaid program' (FinCEN Prepaid Access Final Rule, 76 FR 45403–45420, Vol. 76 No. 146, 29 July 2011 [CORRECTED date, audit defect 8]; threshold at 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(4)(iii)). No FinCEN registration. Residual federal exposure is consumer-protection only: FTC Act § 5 dark-pattern liability over confusing multi-step currency conversions and purchase flows (U.S. v. Epic Games, $245m order finalised March 2023; U.S. v. Cognosphere LLC, $20m, complaint filed 17 Jan 2025, which also barred loot-box sales to under-16s without parental consent), plus COPPA. CAUTION: FinCEN states it 'interprets these exemptions strictly' (FIN-2019-G001 at 9) — the moment a single coin can be cashed out, traded between users, or redeemed for a prize with real value, Model A collapses into Model B.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: Two separate federal problems, one of which is an outright registration requirement. (1) MONEY TRANSMISSION — MANDATORY. A coin that is purchased for dollars, staked player-v-player, and redeemed for cash or prizes of value has 'an equivalent value as currency' and is therefore CVC / 'other value that substitutes for currency' (FIN-2019-G001 § 1.3). The operator issues it and has authority to redeem it, i.e. it is an 'administrator', which FinCEN says generally qualifies as a money transmitter (FIN-2019-G001 § 3, consolidating FIN-2013-G001). FIN-2019-G001 § 4.7 ('CVC Money Transmission Performed by Internet Casinos') is on point for the CVC-denominated version of this design and closes that escape route. CORRECTED QUOTATION (audit defect 5): the guidance reads 'Any person engaged in the business of gambling that is not covered by the regulatory definition of casino, gambling casino, or card club, but accepts and transmits value denominated in CVC, may still be regulated under the BSA as a money transmitter. Indeed, even when the original transmission or the payout are done on a conditional basis (that is, only if a certain event occurs), money transmission under BSA regulations still occurs at the moment the condition is satisfied AND THE ACCEPTANCE OR TRANSMISSION TAKES PLACE.' The original brief truncated the sentence after 'satisfied', dropping the clause that actually bears on whether a duel escrow is transmission at all. Note also that § 4.7 governs only value denominated in CVC; a plain dollar-denominated withdrawable balance is 'funds' and is governed by 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(i)(A) instead. Either way Model B lands in money transmission: the § (ff)(5)(ii)(F) 'integral' exemption is unavailable because moving value between players IS the service. Consequence: FinCEN Form 107 registration within 180 days (31 C.F.R. § 1022.380), written AML programme (31 C.F.R. § 1022.210), SAR filing (31 C.F.R. § 1022.320), recordkeeping, biennial renewal. (2) GAMBLING — DERIVATIVE BUT LIVE. Whether the duel is a 'bet or wager' under § 5362(1)(A) is genuinely unsettled: a head-to-head trivia duel is not a 'contest of others' (the staker is the contestant) and not a 'sporting event', so everything turns on whether it is 'a game subject to chance' — question draw, matchmaking and a 5-second reaction race all inject chance, but there is no federal authority on point. It largely does not matter, because UIGEA only bites where the bet is 'unlawful under any applicable Federal or State law' (§ 5362(10)(A)). Multiple states enacted express dual-currency/sweepstakes bans across 2025-2026 (see subdivisions rows; all secondary-sourced). AUDIT ADDITION (missing item 7): § 5363 is not self-executing against any payee — it prohibits acceptance of payment by 'a person engaged in the business of betting or wagering', and that status is a threshold element the original brief assumed away; § 1084(b) contains a separate safe harbour for transmission of information assisting in the placing of bets between jurisdictions where such betting is legal. Both should be argued before conceding § 5363 / Wire Act exposure. CORRECTED REMEDIES (audit defect 3): criminal penalties for a § 5363 violation — fine and/or up to 5 years — are at 31 U.S.C. § 5366. INJUNCTIVE RELIEF IS AT § 5365 ('Civil remedies'), not § 5366: § 5365 gives district courts original and exclusive jurisdiction to prevent and restrain restricted transactions, authorises a TRO, preliminary injunction or injunction under FRCP 65, and vests standing in the Attorney General, State attorneys general and specified tribal authorities. § 5366 contains no injunction authority. In banned states the operation also becomes an 'illegal gambling business' under 18 U.S.C. § 1955 (state-law violation + 5 or more persons + 30 days or $2,000 in a single day) carrying up to 5 years plus forfeiture. (3) WIRE ACT — probably out (non-sports) under N.H. Lottery Comm'n v. Rosen, 986 F.3d 38 (1st Cir. 20 Jan. 2021), but the 2018 OLC opinion reading § 1084 to cover all wagering has never been formally rescinded by DOJ and is not binding law outside the First Circuit; residual risk is real but low given DOJ's non-enforcement posture since 2021. (4) Federal wagering excise tax: Model B is the model where the excise analysis is genuinely adverse, because player-v-player staking with a rake is the paradigm 'wagering pool ... conducted for profit' and the entry money alone comprises the prize — the exact condition Rev. Rul. 57-521 says makes an entry fee a wager. Verdict: federally you cannot operate Model B without FinCEN MSB registration and a BSA/AML programme — hence 'licence-required' — and you additionally cannot operate it lawfully at all in the growing block of states that have banned the dual-currency structure. This is the highest-risk of the four models by a wide margin.
modelVerdicts.authority: 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(i)(A) and § 1022.380 (current); FinCEN Guidance FIN-2019-G001 §§ 1.3, 3, 4.7 (9 May 2019); 31 U.S.C. §§ 5362(1), 5362(10)(A), 5363, 5365 (civil remedies/injunction), 5366 (criminal penalties) (in force 13 Oct. 2006); 18 U.S.C. § 1955 (in force); 18 U.S.C. § 1084(a) and the § 1084(b) safe harbour, as construed in N.H. Lottery Comm'n v. Rosen, 986 F.3d 38 (1st Cir. 2021); 26 U.S.C. §§ 4401, 4411, 4412, 4421(1)(B) and Rev. Rul. 57-521, 1957-2 C.B. 779

modelVerdicts.reasoning: The intended shelter is 31 U.S.C. § 5362(1)(E)(ix), and it DOES NOT WORK for trivia — this is the most commonly misread provision in the statute. Clause (ix) opens 'participation in any fantasy or simulation sports game or educational game or contest', and founders read 'educational game or contest' as a standalone carve-out. It is not: (ix) imposes three cumulative conditions, and condition (II) requires that 'All winning outcomes reflect the relative knowledge and skill of the participants and are determined predominantly by accumulated statistical results of the performance of individuals (athletes in the case of sports events) in multiple real-world sporting or other events.' A knowledge duel or expedition is not determined by accumulated statistical results of real-world events, so it fails (II) and falls outside (ix) — even though the fixed, pre-announced, entrant-count-independent prize pool satisfies condition (I) perfectly. The stronger federal argument is the threshold one: a paid-entry knowledge contest is arguably not a 'bet or wager' under § 5362(1)(A) at all, because the entrant stakes on their own performance, not on 'a contest of others', not on a sporting event, and — if outcomes are genuinely knowledge-determined — not on 'a game subject to chance'. There is no federal case law resolving this for online trivia. WIRE ACT: § 1084(a) reaches bets 'on any sporting event or contest'; the First Circuit read that phrase as a sports-limited unit (986 F.3d 38), but no other circuit has ruled and the unrescinded 2018 OLC opinion would read 'contest' broadly; the § 1084(b) safe harbour is a further threshold defence (AUDIT ADDITION). IGBA/Travel Act: derivative of state law, i.e. it turns on each state's predominance / material-element / any-chance test — outside this lane. MONEY TRANSMISSION: better than Model B but design-dependent. If the announced prize pool is the operator's own money and is NOT funded by entry fees, the operator is arguably selling a service and paying its own promotional expense, so 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(ii)(F) is available — the position DFS operators take. CORRECTED AUTHORITY (audit defect 5): if you hold a WITHDRAWABLE DOLLAR BALANCE for users, the governing provision is 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(i)(A) (acceptance of currency, funds or other value that substitutes for currency from one person and transmission to another location or person) — NOT FIN-2019-G001 § 4.7, which is a convertible-virtual-currency section and does not reach a dollar balance. Resting the trigger analysis on § 4.7 would misdirect the counsel opinion. Design lever: one-way payouts, no withdrawable stored value. FEDERAL EXCISE TAX — DIRECTION REVERSED BY AUDIT (defects 1 and 2). The original brief called this 'the under-appreciated killer', said § 4421 'draws no skill/chance distinction at all', said the IRS 'has already applied' the tax to paid-entry skill contests, and said the fixed-operator-funded-prize defence was untested with no authority in existence. All four statements are wrong. (a) Rev. Rul. 57-521, 1957-2 C.B. 779 — discussed at length inside AM 2020-009 itself — held that 'contesting for a prize offered by another in a contest of mental or physical skill of the contestant, which the one offering the prize must award in any event, is not gaming; and, the fact that each contestant is required to pay an entrance fee does not make the payment a bet or gaming transaction unless the entrance fees alone comprise the prize'. The ruling concerned a PUZZLE CONTEST with entry fees and guaranteed payments, where 'the operator has obligated itself to pay a sum certain in prizes which is not contingent on the number or amount of entrance fees', and concluded the puzzle game was not a wagering pool or lottery within IRC § 4421. That is directly on point for Model C and is the single most favourable authority in existence for it. (b) AM 2020-009 does say the statutory language 'does not differentiate whether an activity involves skill, chance, or some combination of the two', but the very next sentence reads 'Still, the presence or absence of skill in a contest may help determine whether an entry fee constitutes a taxable wager, or not', and the memo then distinguishes the puzzle contest from DFS: 'In the revenue ruling, the contest participant's own skill was the only factor involved in winning the puzzle game and there was no chance element at all. In contrast, DFS participants merely select a lineup ... and have no ability to exercise control or influence over the actions of the players.' The IRS applied the tax to DFS BECAUSE the entrant does not control the outcome. A trivia duel, where the entrant's own knowledge determines the result, sits on the Rev. Rul. 57-521 side of the line the memo itself draws. (c) The correct residual risk is therefore: the operator-funded, fixed, pre-announced, entrant-count-independent prize is supported by a published revenue ruling that the IRS's own most recent advice endorses; the exposure is that FACT//DUEL's chance elements (question draw, matchmaking, reaction-time scoring) could be argued to pull it toward DFS. AM 2020-009 remains non-precedential (26 U.S.C. § 6110(k)(3)); Rev. Rul. 57-521 is a published revenue ruling and is citable. ADVERTISING / PRIVATE LITIGATION — CORRECTED (audit defect 6): Skillz Platform Inc. v. Papaya Gaming, Ltd., No. 1:24-cv-01646 (S.D.N.Y., Cote, J.) was brought by a COMPETITOR under the Lanham Act and New York General Business Law. FTC Act § 5 has no private right of action and the FTC was not a party. An April 2026 jury returned a $420m verdict; judgment entered 28 July 2026 separately awarded $719 million in disgorgement as an ALTERNATIVE REMEDY THE PLAINTIFF MAY ELECT IN LIEU OF DAMAGES, plus $10.1m in fees — these are alternative, not cumulative. It is a district-court judgment subject to appeal to the Second Circuit, it is not final, and it is NOT precedent and binds no court. The fact pattern — marketing real-money head-to-head 'skill' tournaments while filling them with undisclosed bots — is nonetheless exactly FACT//DUEL's risk if a paying player is ever matched against an AI without unmissable disclosure. Net: genuinely unsettled federally, materially safer than Model B, and the safest of the money-taking models IF the prize is operator-funded, fixed and announced, there is no withdrawable balance, and every opponent is a disclosed human or a disclosed bot.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: A recurring fee for features or cosmetics with no stake and no prize of value engages no federal gambling statute: no 'bet or wager' under 31 U.S.C. § 5362(1)(A), no lottery under 18 U.S.C. §§ 1301-1304, no 'sporting event or contest' wager under 18 U.S.C. § 1084, and nothing for 18 U.S.C. § 1955 to attach to. Not money transmission — the operator accepts funds integral to the sale of its own services (31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(ii)(F)). The live federal law is consumer protection. ROSCA (Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act), 15 U.S.C. §§ 8401-8405, Pub. L. 111-345, requires, for any negative-option feature sold online: clear and conspicuous disclosure of all material terms before obtaining billing information, express informed consent, and simple mechanisms to stop recurring charges (§ 8403). CORRECTED (audit defect 4): the FTC's 2024 AMENDED Negative Option Rule — the 'click-to-cancel' regime — was vacated in its entirety by the Eighth Circuit in Custom Communications, Inc. v. FTC, No. 24-3137 (8th Cir. 8 July 2025), on Magnuson-Moss procedural grounds (failure to conduct a preliminary regulatory analysis after finding annual costs above $100m), days before the 14 July 2025 compliance date. IT IS WRONG TO SAY THERE IS 'NO FTC NEGATIVE OPTION RULE'. The vacatur of the 2024 amendments restored the pre-existing 1973 Prenotification Negative Option Plan rule, still codified at 16 C.F.R. Part 425. The correct statement is that there is currently no click-to-cancel rule, while the narrower 1973 prenotification rule remains on the books — check whether your offer is a prenotification plan within Part 425 before assuming nothing applies. The FTC restarted the rulemaking: a draft ANPRM went to OIRA on 30 January 2026 and the ANPRM WAS PUBLISHED 11 MARCH 2026 with comments due 13 April 2026; per the law-firm account the brief itself relies on, it asks whether to amend the EXISTING Negative Option Rule and separately about certain provisions of the vacated Click-to-Cancel Rule — two distinct instruments. AUDIT ADDITION (missing item 6): STATE AUTOMATIC-RENEWAL LAWS are binding law, not prudence. California's Automatic Renewal Law and New York's and other states' ARLs impose click-to-cancel-equivalent obligations independently of any FTC rule; building to click-to-cancel standards is therefore a compliance requirement in those states, not merely a hedge against the rule returning. Specific state section numbers, effective dates and the current California ARL amendments are UNVERIFIED in this lane and must be confirmed by the state lane or counsel. Also applies: Epic Games/Cognosphere-style dark-pattern liability on the purchase flow, and COPPA if any subscriber could be under 13.

checklist.item: Register as a Money Services Business with FinCEN (FinCEN Form 107, 'Registration of Money Services Business'), filed electronically through the BSA E-Filing System
checklist.issuer: FinCEN (Financial Crimes Enforcement Network), U.S. Department of the Treasury
checklist.appliesTo: B mandatory; C only if you hold withdrawable cash balances for users or the prize pool is entrant-funded; A and D not required
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED (statutory window is 180 days from establishment, not a processing time)
checklist.prerequisite: US legal entity with EIN; named owner/controlling person to sign; BSA E-Filing account
checklist.notes: 31 C.F.R. § 1022.380: file within 180 days after the date the MSB is established; renew every two years on or before 31 December of the second calendar year of each registration period. Re-registration is separately triggered by a change of ownership/control requiring state-law re-registration, a transfer of more than 10% of voting power or equity (for non-SEC reporters), or a >50% increase in the number of agents. CORRECTED TRIGGER AUTHORITY (audit defect 5): the original brief rested the trigger analysis on FinCEN Guidance FIN-2019-G001 § 4.7. That section is titled 'CVC Money Transmission Performed by Internet Casinos' and reaches only a person who 'accepts and transmits value denominated in CVC'. A dollar-denominated withdrawable user balance is plain 'funds', and the governing provision for it is 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(i)(A). Use § 4.7 only for the CVC-denominated variant; do not let counsel be briefed on the wrong provision. NOT LEGAL ADVICE — get a written BSA analysis from US counsel before deciding you are outside this.

checklist.item: Written BSA/AML compliance programme: designated compliance officer, risk-based internal controls, ongoing employee training, independent testing
checklist.issuer: FinCEN / IRS Small Business & Self-Employed Division (the federal examiner for non-bank MSBs)
checklist.appliesTo: B; C if registered as MSB
checklist.notes: 31 C.F.R. § 1022.210. Registration alone is not compliance — the programme, not the form, is what examinations test.

checklist.item: Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) filing capability and procedures
checklist.appliesTo: B; C if registered as MSB
checklist.leadTime: Filing deadline is 30 calendar days after initial detection of facts constituting a basis for filing
checklist.notes: 31 C.F.R. § 1022.320. The dollar threshold for MSB SARs is UNVERIFIED — confirm the current figure in § 1022.320(a)(2) before writing it into procedures.

checklist.appliesTo: B; C if registered as MSB
checklist.leadTime: 15 days after the transaction (verify current deadline)
checklist.notes: 31 C.F.R. § 1010.311, transactions in currency over $10,000. Largely theoretical for a card/ACH-only app — CTRs cover physical currency — but the procedure must exist.

checklist.item: OFAC sanctions screening of users and payouts
checklist.issuer: Office of Foreign Assets Control, U.S. Department of the Treasury
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — any model that moves money
checklist.notes: 31 C.F.R. Chapter V. Strict liability and applies to every US person regardless of MSB status. There is no registration — it is an operational control.

checklist.item: Register for the federal wagering occupational tax before accepting any wagers — IRS Form 11-C, 'Occupational Tax and Registration Return for Wagering'
checklist.appliesTo: B (likely); C only if counsel concludes entry fees are 'wagers' — see corrected analysis, which is now materially FAVOURABLE for an operator-funded fixed-prize contest
checklist.cost: $50 per year where the wager is authorised under the law of the state in which accepted; $500 per year otherwise (26 U.S.C. § 4411)
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED — must be filed before wagers are accepted
checklist.prerequisite: Determination (with counsel) whether entry fees are 'wagers' under 26 U.S.C. § 4421, AND a Fifth Amendment analysis — see below
checklist.notes: 26 U.S.C. §§ 4411, 4412. CORRECTED (audit defects 1 and 2): the original brief said 'skill-vs-chance is irrelevant here' and that the fixed-operator-funded-prize defence was untested with no authority in existence. Both are wrong. Rev. Rul. 57-521, 1957-2 C.B. 779 holds that contesting for a prize offered by another in a contest of mental or physical skill, which the offeror must award in any event, is not gaming, and that an entry fee is not a wager 'unless the entrance fees alone comprise the prize'. AM 2020-009 (23 July 2020) discusses and endorses that ruling, and applied the tax to DFS specifically BECAUSE DFS entrants 'have no ability to exercise control or influence over the actions of the players' — the opposite of a knowledge duel. AM 2020-009 is non-precedential (26 U.S.C. § 6110(k)(3)); Rev. Rul. 57-521 is a published revenue ruling and is citable. AUDIT ADDITION — FIFTH AMENDMENT (missing item 2): registering on Form 11-C at the $500 UNAUTHORISED rate is a public admission of accepting wagers not authorised under the law of the state where accepted, i.e. potential evidence of an 18 U.S.C. § 1955 / state gambling offence. Marchetti v. United States, 390 U.S. 39 (1968) and Grosso v. United States held the self-incrimination privilege a complete defence to prosecution for failure to register/pay the wagering taxes on the then-current scheme; the CURRENT scope of that privilege after subsequent statutory amendments is UNVERIFIED and must be settled with counsel BEFORE anyone files at the unauthorised rate. Do not file blind.

checklist.item: Monthly federal excise tax on wagers — IRS Form 730, 'Monthly Tax Return for Wagers'
checklist.appliesTo: B if entry/stake money is treated as wagers; C only if the Rev. Rul. 57-521 position fails
checklist.cost: 0.25% of the amount wagered if authorised under the law of the state in which accepted; 2% if not (26 U.S.C. § 4401(a))
checklist.notes: 26 U.S.C. § 4401. The 2% rate on unauthorised wagers is applied to HANDLE, not revenue — at scale it can exceed gross margin. Model this before launch. CORRECTED FRAMING: this is a live and severe risk for MODEL B (player-v-player staking with a rake is the paradigm 'wagering pool ... conducted for profit', and the stake money alone comprises the prize — the exact Rev. Rul. 57-521 trigger). For MODEL C with an operator-funded, fixed, pre-announced prize NOT contingent on entrant numbers, the cited authority points the other way. The original brief's 'under-appreciated killer' framing was directionally wrong for Model C.

checklist.item: Prize and winnings information reporting and withholding (Forms W-2G / 1099-MISC; Form 945 for withheld amounts)
checklist.cost: 24% withholding rate under 26 U.S.C. § 3402(q) on certain net winnings of $5,000 or more
checklist.leadTime: Annual information returns; deposits per the withholding schedule
checklist.prerequisite: Collection of payee TIN (Form W-9) before payout
checklist.notes: For calendar year 2026 the minimum reporting threshold for certain information returns including Form W-2G is $2,000 (raised from $600 and inflation-indexed thereafter by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Pub. L. 119-21, enacted 4 July 2025; IRS/Treasury guidance published in the Federal Register 17 April 2026). Which of W-2G versus 1099-MISC applies to a knowledge contest is a real question for your tax counsel — it follows the same 'is this a wagering transaction' analysis as the excise tax. Separately, the same Act amended 26 U.S.C. § 165(d) to cap wagering-loss deductions at 90% of losses from the 2026 tax year. CORRECTED BILL NUMBERS (audit defect 10): the repeal bill is the FAIR BET Act, H.R. 4304 (119th Cong., Rep. Titus, introduced 7 July 2025) — NOT H.R. 6985, which the original brief cited and which could not be confirmed. The House Rules Committee declined to advance it as an NDAA amendment in January 2026 and it had not passed as of September 2026. The FULL HOUSE Act bill number 'S. 2230' remains UNVERIFIED. This is a player-facing communications issue, not an operator obligation.

checklist.item: COPPA compliance programme: neutral age screen before any personal information is collected, direct notice and verifiable parental consent for under-13s, COPPA-compliant privacy policy, data retention/deletion policy, strengthened security requirements
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — all models; unavoidable for a trivia product, which reads as child-attractive
checklist.prerequisite: Decide and document whether the service is child-directed, mixed-audience, or general-audience
checklist.notes: 15 U.S.C. §§ 6501-6506; 16 C.F.R. Part 312. Amended Rule published 22 April 2025, effective 23 June 2025, FULL COMPLIANCE REQUIRED SINCE 22 APRIL 2026 — this is live law today, not a future deadline. Mixed-audience services must age-screen BEFORE collecting personal information, in a neutral manner that does not default to a set age or encourage falsification ('What is your date of birth?', never 'Are you over 13?'). The FTC's 'Enforcement Policy Statement Promoting the Adoption of Age-Verification Technology' of 25 February 2026 is confirmed to exist and is said to give limited relief for data collected solely to run age-verification technology — BUT ITS CONDITIONS AND SCOPE ARE UNVERIFIED IN THIS LANE (audit addition, missing item 5). A money model that hard-blocks under-18s depends on exactly that collection, so read the policy statement in full and confirm the conditions (permitted data categories, retention limits, whether it covers third-party vendors) before relying on it. Practical answer for any money model: hard-block under-18s entirely and document it — state minimum gambling/contest ages make under-18 money play indefensible regardless of COPPA.

checklist.item: FTC Act § 5 and Lanham Act disclosure and purchase-flow review: single-step purchase confirmation, no dark patterns, plain-language coin pricing, disclosure of any AI/bot opponents, disclosure of matchmaking logic, no account lockout for chargeback disputes
checklist.issuer: Federal Trade Commission (and, separately and more dangerously, COMPETITORS suing under the Lanham Act and state UDAP/GBL statutes)

checklist.notes: 15 U.S.C. § 45. Regulator benchmarks: U.S. v. Epic Games (order finalised March 2023, $245m refunds; bars charging via dark patterns and bars locking accounts over disputed charges) and U.S. v. Cognosphere LLC (complaint filed 17 January 2025, C.D. Cal., $20m; bars loot-box sales to under-16s without parental consent and targets confusing multi-step currency conversion). CORRECTED (audit defect 6): Skillz Platform Inc. v. Papaya Gaming, Ltd., No. 1:24-cv-01646 (S.D.N.Y.), Judge Denise Cote, is NOT an FTC Act § 5 or COPPA case — FTC Act § 5 has no private right of action and the FTC was not a party. It was a competitor suit under the LANHAM ACT and NEW YORK GENERAL BUSINESS LAW. An April 2026 jury returned a $420m verdict; the 28 July 2026 judgment separately awarded $719m in disgorgement as an ALTERNATIVE remedy the plaintiff may ELECT IN LIEU OF damages, plus $10.1m in fees — alternative, not cumulative, so '$719m plus $10.1m' as a running total is wrong. It is a district-court judgment, subject to appeal to the Second Circuit, not final, and NOT PRECEDENT anywhere (audit addition, missing item 3). The operational lesson survives all of that: FACT//DUEL's duel mode must never pit a paying player against an AI without unmissable disclosure, and a competitor can bring this claim with no regulator involved at all.

checklist.item: ROSCA-compliant subscription flow: clear and conspicuous disclosure of all material terms before billing information is taken, express informed consent, and a simple cancellation mechanism through the same medium used to subscribe
checklist.appliesTo: D; also A if coin packs auto-renew
checklist.notes: 15 U.S.C. §§ 8403-8404. CORRECTED (audit defect 4): the FTC's 2024 AMENDED Negative Option Rule (the click-to-cancel regime) was vacated in its entirety by the Eighth Circuit in Custom Communications, Inc. v. FTC, No. 24-3137 (8th Cir. 8 July 2025). That vacatur restored the pre-existing 1973 PRENOTIFICATION NEGATIVE OPTION RULE, which REMAINS IN FORCE at 16 C.F.R. Part 425 (audit addition, missing item 4). It is wrong to say 'there is currently no FTC negative option rule' — there is currently no CLICK-TO-CANCEL rule. Check whether your offer is a prenotification plan within Part 425. The FTC restarted the rulemaking: draft ANPRM submitted to OIRA 30 January 2026, ANPRM PUBLISHED 11 MARCH 2026, comments due 13 April 2026; it asks both whether to amend the EXISTING rule and about certain provisions of the vacated click-to-cancel rule. ROSCA and § 5 enforcement continues throughout. Build to click-to-cancel standards regardless — and note that in several states it is not optional (see the state automatic-renewal item below).

checklist.item: AUDIT ADDITION — State automatic-renewal law (ARL) compliance for any subscription: state-specific pre-consent disclosure, affirmative consent capture, acknowledgement/retention of terms, online cancellation mechanism, and renewal reminder notices

That understates the position: several states impose click-to-cancel-equivalent obligations as BINDING LAW independent of any FTC rule, and they survived the Eighth Circuit vacatur untouched. California's Automatic Renewal Law and New York's automatic-renewal provisions are the usual leads; specific code sections, thresholds, reminder-notice intervals and effective dates are UNVERIFIED in this federal lane. Route to the state lane or to counsel before launching any subscription. Treat this as a compliance requirement, not prudence.

risks: STATE-LAW PREEMPTION REALITY — THERE IS NONE. 31 U.S.C. § 5361(b) is an express rule of construction: 'No provision of this subchapter shall be construed as altering, limiting, or extending any Federal or State law or Tribal-State compact prohibiting, permitting, or regulating gambling' in the United States. PASPA was struck down in Murphy v. NCAA (2018), removing the only modern federal attempt to constrain state choice. UIGEA (§ 5362(10)(A)), the Illegal Gambling Business Act (18 U.S.C. § 1955(b)(1)(i)) and the Travel Act (18 U.S.C. § 1952) all take their unlawfulness FROM state law. Clearing the federal layer tells you almost nothing about whether you can operate in any given state.

THE UIGEA 'EDUCATIONAL GAME OR CONTEST' TRAP. § 5362(1)(E)(ix) reads 'participation in any fantasy or simulation sports game or educational game or contest...' and is routinely quoted as if those opening words were a self-contained carve-out for quiz products. They are not. Clause (ix) imposes three cumulative conditions, and (ix)(II) requires outcomes 'determined predominantly by accumulated statistical results of the performance of individuals ... in multiple real-world sporting or other events'. No trivia game can satisfy that. If any adviser tells the founder that FACT//DUEL is a UIGEA-exempt 'educational contest', that adviser has misread the statute.

CORRECTED RISK — THE FEDERAL WAGERING EXCISE TAX IS A MODEL B PROBLEM, NOT A MODEL C KILLER. The original brief said this was 'the most likely way this product loses money quietly', that § 4421 'makes no skill/chance distinction', and that AM 2020-009 applied §§ 4401/4411 to DFS 'on exactly that basis'. The audit refuted all three at 'certain' confidence and this pass adopts the refutation. AM 2020-009 states the statute 'does not differentiate whether an activity involves skill, chance, or some combination of the two' and then immediately says 'Still, the presence or absence of skill in a contest may help determine whether an entry fee constitutes a taxable wager, or not', distinguishing DFS from Rev. Rul. 57-521's puzzle contest on the ground that the DFS entrant 'has no ability to exercise control or influence over the actions of the players'. Rev. Rul. 57-521, 1957-2 C.B. 779 holds that an entry fee in a contest of mental skill with a guaranteed operator-funded prize is not a wager 'unless the entrance fees alone comprise the prize'. WHAT REMAINS TRUE: the 2% unauthorised rate is levied on HANDLE, not net revenue, so IF the analysis goes against you the tax can exceed gross margin — model it. But for Model C with an operator-funded fixed prize the leading authority is favourable, and for Model B (stake money alone comprising the prize) it is adverse. The risk is Model B's, and the residual Model C risk is that chance elements — question draw, matchmaking, reaction-time scoring — pull the product toward the DFS side of the line the IRS itself drew.

AUDIT ADDITION — DO NOT FILE FORM 11-C WITHOUT A FIFTH AMENDMENT ANALYSIS. The checklist tells the founder to register before accepting any wagers, and the $500 rate applies where wagers are NOT authorised under the law of the state where accepted. Filing at that rate is a signed, dated federal admission of accepting unauthorised wagers — i.e. potential evidence in a 18 U.S.C. § 1955 or state gambling prosecution. Marchetti v. United States, 390 U.S. 39 (1968) and Grosso v. United States held the self-incrimination privilege a complete defence to failure-to-register/pay prosecutions under the then-existing wagering tax scheme. The CURRENT scope of the privilege after later amendments to §§ 4411/4412 is UNVERIFIED here. Settle it with counsel before filing. A compliance step that manufactures the evidence for a criminal case is not a compliance step.

MODEL A DEGRADES INTO MODEL B ON A SINGLE PRODUCT DECISION. One cash-out path, one peer-to-peer coin transfer, one 'redeem coins for a gift card' feature, or one tournament that pays a prize of value, and the coin becomes convertible virtual currency, FinCEN money-transmitter obligations attach, and the state sweepstakes bans engage. FinCEN 'interprets these exemptions strictly' (FIN-2019-G001 at 9). Put a hard architectural boundary — not a policy note — between the closed-loop coin and anything redeemable. Note also the corrected authority position: once coins are SOLD, § 5362(1)(E)(viii) stops protecting them, so Model A's only remaining federal argument is 'no prize of value' under § 5362(1)(A). That argument fails the instant anything of value is paid out.

THE WIRE ACT IS NARROW BUT NOT SETTLED NATIONWIDE. N.H. Lottery Comm'n v. Rosen, 986 F.3d 38 (1st Cir. 20 Jan. 2021) limits 18 U.S.C. § 1084 to sporting events, and DOJ did not seek certiorari. But the 2018 OLC opinion reading § 1084 to cover all interstate wagering has never been formally withdrawn, and the First Circuit's holding binds only Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Puerto Rico. In the other circuits there is no controlling authority. AUDIT ADDITION: the § 1084(b) safe harbour (transmission of information for use in news reporting, and transmission between jurisdictions where the betting is legal) is a threshold defence the original analysis skipped. Treat the Wire Act as low-probability, high-severity tail risk rather than a resolved question.

CORRECTED — BOTS AND MATCHMAKING ARE A NINE-FIGURE PRIVATE-LITIGATION RISK, BROUGHT BY COMPETITORS, NOT REGULATORS, AND NOT YET FINAL. Skillz Platform Inc. v. Papaya Gaming, Ltd., No. 1:24-cv-01646 (S.D.N.Y., Cote, J.) produced a $420m April 2026 jury verdict; the 28 July 2026 judgment separately awarded $719m in DISGORGEMENT as an ALTERNATIVE remedy the plaintiff may elect IN LIEU OF damages, plus $10.1m in fees. The figures are alternative, not cumulative — the original brief's headline '$719m' and checklist '$719m plus $10.1m' read as a running total and overstate the award. The claims were under the LANHAM ACT and NEW YORK GENERAL BUSINESS LAW, not FTC Act § 5 or COPPA; the FTC was not a party and FTC Act § 5 has no private right of action. It is a district-court judgment, subject to appeal to the Second Circuit, NOT FINAL, and NOT PRECEDENT anywhere. What survives every one of those corrections: the conduct found — marketing real-money 'skill-based head-to-head' tournaments while secretly filling them with bots — is precisely FACT//DUEL's exposure. The product currently has no server and no real opponents; whatever fills a duel must be audited and disclosed before a single dollar is staked. A competitor can bring this claim with no regulator interest at all.

MSB REGISTRATION IS NOT A LICENCE AND WILL NOT SATISFY THE STATES. FinCEN Form 107 is a federal registration with no approval step. It does not authorise money transmission in any state. Roughly every state requires its own money transmitter licence with bonding and net-worth requirements — a multi-year, multi-million-dollar programme that is outside this federal lane but is the real cost driver for Models B and C. It is now a checklist item (audit addition), not merely a narrative aside.

HOLDING USER BALANCES IS THE SINGLE DESIGN CHOICE THAT MOST CHANGES THE LEGAL ANSWER. A withdrawable cash balance makes the operator look like a money transmitter under 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(i)(A) — which is the correct provision for dollar-denominated value, not FIN-2019-G001 § 4.7 — even where the game itself is defensible. One-way payouts (money in, contest entered, prize paid out directly to the winner's funding instrument, no stored redeemable value) preserve the 'integral to the sale of services' exemption at § 1010.100(ff)(5)(ii)(F). This is worth designing around from day one and is the highest-leverage single decision in the whole file.

COPPA IS ALREADY IN FULL FORCE, NOT PENDING. The amended Rule's compliance date passed on 22 April 2026. A trivia product with cartoon-adjacent presentation, no accounts and no age gate is a plausible FTC target on child-directedness alone, entirely independently of anything to do with money. The FTC's 25 February 2026 age-verification enforcement policy statement is confirmed to exist but its CONDITIONS ARE UNVERIFIED — a hard under-18 block depends on collecting exactly the data that statement addresses, so read it before designing the gate.

AUDIT ADDITION — MODEL D IS NOT A CONSUMER-PROTECTION FREE PASS. Two corrections compound here: the 1973 Prenotification Negative Option Rule survived the click-to-cancel vacatur and remains at 16 C.F.R. Part 425, and state automatic-renewal laws (California, New York and others) impose click-to-cancel-equivalent duties as binding law. 'Federally lawful' plus 'build to click-to-cancel standards anyway' understated both. Model D is the cheapest model to launch and the easiest one to get sued over for a bad cancellation flow.

FEDERAL CLEARANCE ON MODEL A OR D DOES NOT MAKE THE CURRENT PRODUCT FUTURE-PROOF. The existing FREE demo-coin game sits squarely inside 31 U.S.C. § 5362(1)(E)(viii)(II) — 'points or credits that the sponsor of the game or contest provides to participants free of charge and that can be used or redeemed only for participation in games or contests offered by the sponsor'. That exclusion is written around free credits and it stops applying the moment coins are sold for money. It therefore protects today's product and none of the four proposed models.

AUDIT ADDITION — § 5363 HAS A THRESHOLD THE ORIGINAL ANALYSIS ASSUMED AWAY. 31 U.S.C. § 5363 prohibits acceptance of payment by 'a person engaged in the business of betting or wagering' in connection with unlawful internet gambling. Whether FACT//DUEL is such a person is a contestable element, not a given, particularly for Model C. Do not concede it. Argue the threshold before arguing the exclusions.

uncertain: Whether a head-to-head trivia duel is 'a game subject to chance' within 31 U.S.C. § 5362(1)(A). No federal case law located on online knowledge games. The question-draw, matchmaking and 5/7/10-second reaction race all introduce chance elements; a court could go either way. Needs a reasoned counsel opinion, not a guess. This is the same factual question that decides whether the Rev. Rul. 57-521 excise position holds — the two stand or fall together.

CORRECTED FROM 'UNTESTED': whether a fixed, pre-announced, operator-funded prize escapes 'wagering pool ... conducted for profit' under 26 U.S.C. § 4421(1)(B) is NOT unsupported. Rev. Rul. 57-521, 1957-2 C.B. 779 is directly on point and favourable, and AM 2020-009 endorses it. What remains genuinely uncertain is (a) whether FACT//DUEL's chance elements take it outside the ruling, and (b) whether the IRS would apply the ruling to a modern app. I have NOT read Rev. Rul. 57-521 in its original form — only the extensive quotation of it inside AM 2020-009 via the audit. Pull the ruling text before relying on it.

Whether Model C prize payouts are reported on Form W-2G or Form 1099-MISC. This follows the same 'is it a wagering transaction' analysis and no IRS guidance addressing knowledge contests specifically was found.

The exact 2026 information-reporting threshold as it applies to each form. A $2,000 figure for calendar year 2026 was taken from the IRS Instructions for Forms W-2G and 5754 (Rev. January 2026) and the Federal Register listing of 17 April 2026, but the full Federal Register document was not read and the code sections beyond W-2G were not independently confirmed. Confirm before configuring tax reporting.

corrections: CERTAIN / fabricated — Rev. Rul. 57-521, 1957-2 C.B. 779 ADDED and the Model C excise-tax conclusion REVERSED IN DIRECTION. The brief claimed no ruling, case or IRS guidance tested whether a fixed, pre-announced, operator-funded prize escapes § 4421(1)(B). The ruling is quoted at length inside the very memo the brief cites (AM 2020-009): contesting for a prize offered by another in a contest of mental or physical skill which the offeror must award in any event is not gaming, and an entry fee is not a wager 'unless the entrance fees alone comprise the prize'; where 'the operator has obligated itself to pay a sum certain in prizes which is not contingent on the number or amount of entrance fees', the contest is not a wagering pool within § 4421. This is the strongest authority in existence for Model C and the brief said it did not exist.

CERTAIN / overstated — the claim that the IRS 'has already applied' the excise tax to paid-entry skill contests 'regardless of skill-vs-chance', and that '§ 4421 draws no skill/chance distinction at all', REMOVED from the headline, Model C and the risks. AM 2020-009 says the statute does not differentiate by skill or chance and then immediately adds 'Still, the presence or absence of skill in a contest may help determine whether an entry fee constitutes a taxable wager, or not', distinguishing DFS on the ground that DFS entrants 'have no ability to exercise control or influence over the actions of the players'. The IRS taxed DFS BECAUSE the entrant does not control the outcome. A knowledge duel sits on the other side of that line. 'The under-appreciated killer' framing is withdrawn for Model C and re-aimed at Model B.

CERTAIN / misattributed — injunctive relief for a UIGEA violation moved from 31 U.S.C. § 5366 to § 5365. § 5365 ('Civil remedies') gives district courts original and exclusive jurisdiction to prevent and restrain restricted transactions, authorises TRO/preliminary injunction/injunction under FRCP 65, and vests standing in the Attorney General, State attorneys general and specified tribal authorities. § 5366 is criminal penalties only (fine and/or up to 5 years) and contains no injunction authority.

CERTAIN / outdated — FinCEN Prepaid Access Final Rule citation corrected to 76 FR 45403-45420, Vol. 76 No. 146, 29 JULY 2011. The brief paired the FR page with 26 July 2011, which is the date of FinCEN's two-page press release — and the press-release URL was in fact what the brief listed in its sources as the rule. Both the date and the source URL are fixed; the substantive $2,000/day closed-loop threshold at 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(4)(iii) was correct and is retained.

LIKELY / misattributed — Skillz v. Papaya reclassified. Removed from the 'FTC Act § 5 / COPPA' federal gate: it was a COMPETITOR suit under the Lanham Act and New York GBL; FTC Act § 5 has no private right of action and the FTC was not a party. Removed the word 'precedent': it is an S.D.N.Y. district-court judgment entered 28 July 2026, subject to appeal to the Second Circuit, not final, binding no court. Corrected the money: the $719m disgorgement is an ALTERNATIVE remedy the plaintiff may elect IN LIEU OF the $420m April 2026 jury verdict, so '$719m plus $10.1m fees' as a cumulative total is wrong.

LIKELY / misattributed — the money-transmission trigger for a DOLLAR-denominated withdrawable user balance moved off FinCEN Guidance FIN-2019-G001 § 4.7 and onto 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(i)(A). § 4.7 is titled 'CVC Money Transmission Performed by Internet Casinos' and reaches only a person who 'accepts and transmits value denominated in CVC'; the whole of FIN-2019-G001 is convertible-virtual-currency guidance. Also restored the truncated quotation: the sentence ends 'at the moment the condition is satisfied AND THE ACCEPTANCE OR TRANSMISSION TAKES PLACE' — the brief closed the quotation after 'satisfied', dropping the clause that bears on whether a duel escrow is transmission at all.
